page.emptyHint: Record scoliosis angle and shoulder symmetry

card.summaryFallback: Spine, shoulder, pelvis, and lower-limb alignment assessment

early.heading: Posture issues are better found early
early.body: Scoliosis, uneven shoulders, kyphosis, and similar posture issues are more likely to appear or progress during rapid growth (ages 6-14). When noticed early, exercise intervention and posture correction may help; when noticed late, bracing or surgery may be needed.

regularObservation.label: Observe regularly
regularObservation.desc: Do a simple at-home posture screen every 3-6 months and record it so changes can be compared over time.

signalWatch.label: Watch daily signals
signalWatch.desc: Notice whether the child tilts their head while writing, sits crookedly, has a backpack that keeps sliding to one side, or has one side of the collar sitting higher.

checkupData.label: Use checkup data
checkupData.desc: Enter school spine-screening results promptly, and always record Cobb angle data when it is available.

preparation.heading: Preparation
preparation.body: Have the child wear fitted clothing or expose the back, then stand naturally in a well-lit place. Feet together, arms relaxed at the sides, eyes forward. Do not ask them to force the chest up or shrug.

shoulder.label: 1. Check shoulders
shoulder.desc: Stand directly behind the child and compare the highest point of each shoulder. If one side is clearly higher, record left high or right high. If they are roughly level, choose symmetric.

scapula.label: 2. Check shoulder blades
scapula.desc: Observe whether the shoulder blades are symmetric. One side protruding or winging may suggest spinal rotation. Take a phone photo for reference.

adam.label: 3. Forward bend test (Adam test)
adam.desc: Ask the child to put both feet together, bend forward slowly, and let the arms hang naturally. From behind, compare whether both sides of the back are level. A clear rib hump on one side may suggest spinal rotation or scoliosis. This is the most common school-screening method.

symmetry.label: 4. Check overall symmetry
symmetry.desc: Observe whether the head is centered, both waist lines are symmetric, and the pelvis is level. From the front, compare whether the armpit triangles are symmetric.

photo.heading: Photo guidance
photo.body: Each time you observe, take one standing photo from the rear, left side, and right side, plus one photo during the forward bend test. Keep distance and angle consistent so future comparison is easier. Add notes in the remarks field when useful.

definition.heading: What Cobb angle is
definition.body: Cobb angle is the key quantitative measure for scoliosis. It is measured from a spinal X-ray and represents the size of the curve. A larger value means a larger curve. It is not estimated by eye; a doctor must measure it from the X-ray.

normal.note: Mild spinal asymmetry can be normal and usually does not need intervention

mild.note: Observe regularly and review every 6 months. Strengthen core muscles

moderate.note: Orthotic bracing may be needed, especially before skeletal maturity. Review every 3-6 months

severe.note: Surgery may be considered. Ongoing specialist follow-up is needed

source.heading: Where the data comes from
source.body: Prioritize Cobb angle values from school spine-screening forms, hospital checkup reports, or orthopedic assessments. If there has been no X-ray exam, leave this blank. Shoulder-symmetry records are still useful.

why.heading: Why foot arch matters
why.body: The foot arch is the foot's natural spring for cushioning and support. Children's arches usually form gradually from ages 3-6, and some flatness before age 6 can be normal. If flat feet remain obvious after age 6, walking tires easily, or knock-knees or in-toeing appear, it deserves attention.

prepare.label: 1. Prepare
prepare.desc: Prepare dark cardboard or a dry tile floor. Have the child step in water barefoot so the soles are wet.

observe.label: 2. Step and print
observe.desc: Have the child stand naturally on the cardboard with normal weight bearing, then lift the feet and check the footprint.

compare.label: 3. Read the print
compare.desc: Normal arch: the middle footprint has a clear curved gap, about one third to one half of foot width. Flat foot: the footprint is almost a full sole shape with little middle gap. High arch: the middle gap is too large, with only heel and forefoot marks.

wear.label: Check sole wear
wear.desc: Normal wear is usually heavier on the outer heel. Heavy inner-side wear may suggest flat foot or foot valgus.

fatigue.label: Check standing posture
fatigue.desc: From behind, observe whether the Achilles tendon is vertical while the child stands. A clear inward tilt may suggest foot valgus.

gait.label: Ask how it feels
gait.desc: After long walks or exercise, do the feet hurt easily or do the legs feel sore? That may signal insufficient arch support.

dataSource.heading: Data source
dataSource.body: Foot-arch status in the posture profile is automatically read from fitness assessments, so it does not need to be entered here again. If no foot-arch data exists yet, add it on the fitness assessment page first.

shoulderOrWaist.label: Abnormal forward bend test
shoulderOrWaist.desc: One side of the back clearly rises during forward bending. Even a mild finding is worth further examination.

adamProminence.label: Persistent shoulder asymmetry
adamProminence.desc: Repeated observations show clear uneven shoulders, especially with a worsening trend.

cobbProgress.label: Cobb angle ≥ 10°
cobbProgress.desc: A screening or checkup finds a Cobb angle of 10° or higher, which needs regular follow-up.

cobbRapidIncrease.label: Rapid Cobb angle increase
cobbRapidIncrease.desc: An increase of more than 5° within six months suggests progression and needs active intervention.

footArch.label: Obvious flat feet after age 6
footArch.desc: Walking tires easily, frequent foot or leg soreness, or heavy inner-side sole wear should be assessed by orthopedics or a foot and ankle specialist.

department.heading: Which department to visit
department.body: For spine concerns, start with orthopedics or spine surgery; some hospitals have dedicated scoliosis clinics. For foot arch concerns, orthopedics or foot and ankle surgery can help, or rehabilitation can assess movement correction and orthotic insole plans.

growthSpurt.title: Pay special attention during rapid growth
growthSpurt.body: Around puberty (girls ages 10-14, boys ages 12-16) is when scoliosis can progress fastest. If scoliosis is found during this period, the review interval is often shortened to every 3 months.

PO-OBS-CONC-001.0: Choose a time today when your child is playing independently. Sit nearby quietly for 10 minutes without interrupting or guiding; just observe.
PO-OBS-CONC-001.1: Place two or three materials on the table, let your child choose, and notice how long they stay engaged.
PO-OBS-CONC-001.2: Next time your child is focused, notice whether you feel an urge to interrupt, and try holding back.
PO-OBS-CONC-001.3: If your child is repeating an activity, do not stop them. Wait until they finish, then record their expression.

PO-OBS-EMOT-001.0: When your child is upset today, crouch down to eye level and wait 10 seconds before speaking.
PO-OBS-EMOT-001.1: Before bed, recall the day together: what was the happiest moment, and was anything upsetting?
PO-OBS-EMOT-001.2: Next time your child cries, try saying only "I am here" and notice their response.
PO-OBS-EMOT-001.3: Name feelings together: "Do you feel angry or hurt right now?"

PO-OBS-SOCL-001.0: Take your child somewhere with peers and observe how they join, watch, or avoid interaction.
PO-OBS-SOCL-001.1: Next time your child has a conflict with another child, wait 30 seconds and see whether they can work it out.
PO-OBS-SOCL-001.2: Set up a turn-taking game at home and observe how your child responds while waiting.
PO-OBS-SOCL-001.3: Ask your child, "Who did you play with today? What did you do together?" and notice how they describe it.

PO-OBS-CHOI-001.0: Offer your child two choices today instead of asking "what do you want to do," and observe how they decide.
PO-OBS-CHOI-001.1: Let your child choose what to wear today without evaluating the choice.
PO-OBS-CHOI-001.2: Next time your child says "I do not want to," ask, "What would you like instead?"
PO-OBS-CHOI-001.3: Prepare three books and let your child choose one for bedtime. Watch the choice process.

PO-OBS-INDP-001.0: Choose one thing your child is close to doing independently, such as putting on shoes. Wait nearby today without helping.
PO-OBS-INDP-001.1: Let your child pour water or serve food, even if some spills, and first watch how they handle it.
PO-OBS-INDP-001.2: Before going out, give your child 5 minutes to prepare independently and see what they remember to bring.
PO-OBS-INDP-001.3: If your child says "I cannot do it," try saying "Give it a try first. I am right here."

PO-OBS-RELQ-001.0: Try 10 minutes tonight of being together without looking at your phone. Let your child decide what you do.
PO-OBS-RELQ-001.1: Next time your child speaks, put down what you are holding, crouch down, listen fully, then respond.
PO-OBS-RELQ-001.2: Before bed, offer one specific affirmation: "You put the toys away by yourself today. I appreciated that."
PO-OBS-RELQ-001.3: After a conflict with your child, initiate repair: "My tone was not good just now. I am sorry."
PO-OBS-RELQ-001.4: Ask your child an open question today: "What was something interesting at school today?"

PO-OBS-ATTC-001.0: Before leaving, use a consistent goodbye ritual such as a high five, hug, or special phrase, and watch the separation response.
PO-OBS-ATTC-001.1: When your child explores a new environment, sit somewhere visible without rushing them, and notice whether they look back to check you are there.
PO-OBS-ATTC-001.2: Next time your child cries after feeling wronged, offer a hug first without rushing to ask "what happened?"
PO-OBS-ATTC-001.3: Create a private "safe signal" together that your child can use when they feel uncomfortable.

PO-OBS-EXEC-001.0: Let your child plan tomorrow: what comes first and what comes next. Review the plan together in the evening.
PO-OBS-EXEC-001.1: Next time your child delays homework, ask, "How long do you think this will take?"
PO-OBS-EXEC-001.2: Give your child a task with more than one step, such as "wash your hands, then bring bowls and chopsticks to the table," and observe the process.
PO-OBS-EXEC-001.3: When your child forgets something, do not solve it for them immediately. Ask, "What could help you remember next time?"

PO-REM-REL-001.0: When your child cried or called for you today, about how long did it take you to respond?
PO-REM-REL-001.1: How did your child's emotion change after you responded?

PO-REM-REL-002.0: Was there a moment today when your child explored or played independently while you stayed nearby without intervening?
PO-REM-REL-002.1: When your child met difficulty during exploration, what did you do?

PO-REM-REL-003.0: What did your child want to do independently today?
PO-REM-REL-003.1: How did you respond to "I can do it myself," and what happened?

PO-REM-REL-004.0: The last time your child made a mistake, what was the first thing you said?
PO-REM-REL-004.1: How did your child respond? If you could replay it, what would you say?

PO-REM-REL-005.0: Have you and your child had a conflict recently? How did you reconnect afterward?

PO-REM-REL-006.0: This week, how much of your conversation with your child was about schoolwork, and how much was about what interests them?

guide.title: What is Tanner staging?
guide.description: Tanner staging is an internationally used puberty assessment standard. It divides {{bodySystem}} and pubic hair development into 5 stages each.
guide.howToJudgeFemale: Observe breast size, shape, and areola changes. B1 is prepubertal with no development. B2, the breast bud stage, means a small firm area appears under the nipple and is often the first puberty signal. If B2 appears before age 8, consult a professional to rule out precocious puberty.
guide.howToJudgeMale: Observe testicular size and penile length changes. G1 is prepubertal. G2 means the testes begin to enlarge, usually measured with an orchidometer at more than 4 mL. If G2 appears before age 9, consult a professional to rule out precocious puberty.
guide.primaryAttentionFemale: If it appears before age 8, consult a professional
guide.primaryAttentionMale: If it appears before age 9, consult a professional
guide.pubicHairTimingMale: Usually appears at the same time as G2 or soon after
guide.pubicHairNote: Isolated early pubic hair may reflect premature adrenarche
guide.medicalEarlyFemale: Breast development (B2) before age 8 may indicate precocious puberty
guide.medicalEarlyMale: Testicular enlargement (G2) before age 9 may indicate precocious puberty
guide.medicalDelayFemale: No development signs by age 13 may indicate delayed puberty
guide.medicalDelayMale: No development signs by age 14 may indicate delayed puberty
guide.medicalRapidProgress: Development progresses too quickly, such as crossing 2 stages within 1 year, or is accompanied by accelerated height growth
guide.medicalBoneAge: Use bone age assessment to help evaluate developmental progress

1.title: B1 · Prepubertal
1.desc: Only the nipple is slightly raised; there is no breast tissue development, similar to early childhood.
1.howToJudge: 👀 Observe: the chest is flat as in childhood. Gently touch under the nipple; there should be no firm lump.

2.title: B2 · Breast bud
2.desc: A small firm lump appears under the nipple, about coin-sized, with slight areola enlargement. This is often the first puberty signal.
2.howToJudge: 👆 Palpate: press gently under the nipple with the fingertip. A small firm nodule about 1-2 cm may be felt. The areola may be slightly darker and larger. If this appears before age 8, consult a professional to rule out precocious puberty.

3.title: B3 · Mid development
3.desc: The breast is visibly raised beyond the chest wall from the side, while the areola and breast still form one smooth contour.
3.howToJudge: 👀 Side view: the breast clearly protrudes from the chest wall, but the areola has not formed a separate mound. The outline remains a smooth curve.

4.title: B4 · Areola mound
4.desc: The areola and nipple form a second small mound, like a smaller hill on the breast.
4.howToJudge: 👀 Front view: the areola area protrudes as a small disc above the breast, creating a two-layer appearance. Not every girl goes through this stage clearly.

5.title: B5 · Mature stage
5.desc: The breast has an adult contour. The areola has receded into the breast contour and only the nipple projects.
5.howToJudge: 👀 Observe: the breast has a mature rounded contour. The areola that protruded in B4 has receded and blends into the breast surface, with only the nipple projecting.

1.title: G1 · Prepubertal
1.desc: The testes, scrotum, and penis look the same as in early childhood. Testicular volume is under 4 mL.
1.howToJudge: 📏 Reference: the testes are close to peanut size (long axis under 2.5 cm, about 1-3 mL). The scrotal skin is light in color and similar in texture to nearby skin.

2.title: G2 · Early stage
2.desc: The testes begin to enlarge (volume at least 4 mL), usually the first puberty signal for boys. The penis has not changed much yet.
2.howToJudge: 📏 Reference: the testes grow from peanut size to about grape size (long axis about 2.5-3 cm, about 4-6 mL). The scrotal skin begins to thin and redden. The penis itself has not lengthened yet. If this appears before age 9, consult a professional to rule out precocious puberty.

3.title: G3 · Mid development
3.desc: The penis begins to lengthen, without much thickening yet, and the testes continue to enlarge to about 8-10 mL.
3.howToJudge: 📏 Reference: the testes are about longan or cherry size (long axis about 3-3.5 cm, about 8-10 mL). The penis is clearly longer than before, while thickness changes are still limited.

4.title: G4 · Near mature
4.desc: The penis grows further and thickens, the glans is more distinct, and the testes are about 12-15 mL.
4.howToJudge: 📏 Reference: the testes are about chestnut size (long axis about 4-4.5 cm, about 12-15 mL). The penis is both longer and thicker. The glans contour is clear and scrotal color is noticeably darker.

5.title: G5 · Mature stage
5.desc: External genitalia have reached adult size. Testicular volume is about 15-25 mL.
5.howToJudge: 📏 Reference: the testes are about jujube or small egg size (long axis about 4.5-5 cm, about 15-25 mL). Overall external genital appearance is adult-like.

1.title: PH1 · No pubic hair
1.desc: There is no pubic hair in the genital area, only fine vellus hair similar to the abdomen.
1.howToJudge: 👀 Observe: it looks like childhood, with only very fine light vellus hair that is barely visible.

2.title: PH2 · Sparse appearance
2.desc: A small amount of longer, slightly darker hair appears, usually along the labia or at the base of the penis.
2.howToJudge: 👀 Observe: a few to a dozen longer, slightly darker hairs may be visible. They are usually straight or slightly curved and mainly appear on the perineum or at the base of the penis.

3.title: PH3 · More and coarser
3.desc: Hair becomes more numerous, coarser, curlier, darker, and starts spreading toward the pubic area.
3.howToJudge: 👀 Observe: there is enough hair to describe as a small cluster. It starts curling, becomes clearly dark, and spreads toward the lower abdomen.

4.title: PH4 · Near adult
4.desc: Hair texture is close to adult pubic hair: coarse and curly, with wider coverage but not yet extending to the inner thighs.
4.howToJudge: 👀 Observe: the hair is dense and adult-like in texture, coarse and curly, but the distribution has not yet reached the inner upper thighs.

5.title: PH5 · Adult pattern
5.desc: Hair distribution and density are adult-like, extending to the inner thighs; typically inverted-triangle in females and diamond-shaped in males.
5.howToJudge: 👀 Observe: distribution and density are adult-like and extend to the inner upper thighs.

what.heading: What is refraction?
what.body: Refraction checks the eye's refractive state: myopia, hyperopia, astigmatism, or emmetropia. Clinics usually issue a refraction sheet.

small.label: Undilated refraction
small.desc: Refraction in the natural state, without dilation drops. Common for routine reviews; fast, but accommodation can affect the result.

cycloplegic.label: Dilated refraction
cycloplegic.desc: Refraction after drops that relax the ciliary muscle, helping exclude pseudomyopia. Often used for first prescriptions or teenagers.

computer.label: Autorefraction
computer.desc: Measured automatically by an autorefractor and printed as a slip. Sphere is marked S or SPH; cylinder is marked C or CYL. Fast, but for reference only.

subjective.label: Subjective refraction
subjective.desc: The clinician adjusts lenses step by step while the child identifies targets. Also called subjective refraction. Sphere may be marked DS and cylinder DC. This is more accurate for prescriptions.

sph.note: Negative means myopia; positive means hyperopia. For example, -1.25 means 125 degrees of myopia.

cyl.note: Usually negative. For example, -0.75 means 75 degrees of astigmatism. If there is no astigmatism, it may be 0 or omitted.

axis.note: An angle between 0 and 180°. It is meaningful only when astigmatism is present.

va.note: For example, -> 1.0 means the corrected vision reaches 1.0.

pd.note: Needed for glasses fitting; this app does not record it yet.

eyeNames.heading: What are OD and OS?
eyeNames.body: OD means right eye (Oculus Dexter), and OS means left eye (Oculus Sinister). Some sheets use R (Right) and L (Left). Pay attention to the side when entering data.

examples.heading: Common format examples
examples.odFull: Right eye: 125 degrees myopia / 75 degrees astigmatism, axis 80°, corrected vision 1.0.
examples.shortNotation: No DS/DC suffix is shown; the meaning is the same.
examples.plano: Plano PL means both sphere and cylinder are 0; enter 0 for both.
examples.uncorrectedPrefix: The first number, 0.6, is uncorrected visual acuity.

what.heading: What is axial biometry?
what.body: Axial length (AL) is the distance from cornea to retina and is a core indicator for predicting myopia progression. Each 1mm of axial growth is roughly equivalent to 300 degrees of myopia. It is more predictive than a visual-acuity chart alone.

fields.heading: Fields on an axial biometry sheet

al.note: Normal adults are about 24mm. Children should be below same-age averages. Values beyond the threshold need close attention.

k2.note: Usually about 43-45D. The difference between K1 and K2 reflects corneal astigmatism.

acd.note: Distance from cornea to the front surface of the lens, usually about 2.5-4.0mm.

lt.note: Thickness of the intraocular lens, usually about 3.5-4.5mm.

reserve.heading: Axial reserve
reserve.body: Axial reserve = same-age, same-sex axial threshold minus the child's current axial length. The smaller the reserve, the higher the myopia risk. At each check, axial growth speed matters more than the absolute value. Growth above 0.3mm per half year needs attention.
